title: RocketEval: Efficient Automated LLM Evaluation via Grading Checklist
authors: Tianjun Wei*, Wei Wen*, Ruizhi Qiao, Xing Sun, Jianghong Ma (* equal contribution; Wei as an intern at Tencent; Qiao and Ma corresponding)
lab: Tencent Youtu Lab, City University of Hong Kong, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)
date: 7 March 2025 (arXiv v1, the only version); OpenReview publication 22 January 2025

code.title: Joinn99/RocketEval-ICLR
code.note: MIT-licensed code: checklist creation, grading through vLLM or any OpenAI-compatible API, the score predictor and rankings; data (queries, checklists, responses, GPT-4o labels and a few example gradings) on Hugging Face as Joinn/RocketEval. About 20 minutes for the README and score.py

takeaway: Move the judgment out of the judge: a frontier model compiles each query into 5-10 binary checklist questions once, then a 2B model answers them independently and you read the normalised Yes/No logit instead of the generated token, killing positional bias and preserving calibration; Gemma-2-2B hits 0.965 Spearman with Arena Elo (Mistral-Nemo 0.986, above GPT-4o's 0.979) at $27.70 per 1,000 tests versus $3,400, though instance-level agreement stays at 57.9% versus a 64.7% human ceiling.
verdict: Believe the diagnosis and the cost arithmetic: both check out against the released data. Read "comparable to GPT-4o" as a claim about ranking 12 hand-picked, well-separated models, where 0.965 against 0.979 is one discordant pair out of 66; on single responses the small judges stay well short of humans and of GPT-4o.

headline.k: Gemma-2-2B as judge: its WildBench ranking of 12 models against Chatbot Arena Elo
headline.d: GPT-4o's own ranking scores 0.979; the gap is one discordant pair of 66

headline.k: the whole WildBench benchmark graded 1,000 times by Gemma-2-2B, checklists included
headline.d: against $3,400 with GPT-4o at batch prices: 123 times cheaper (Llama-3-8B: 48 times)

headline.k: Gemma-2-2B with RocketEval against individual MT-Bench human votes
headline.d: up from 37.9% with chain of thought; humans agree with each other 64.7%, GPT-4o 66.6%

resources.t: WildBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Challenging Tasks from Real Users in the Wild
resources.n: the benchmark whose 1,024 real queries, per-query checklists and GPT-4o grades RocketEval builds on; its checklist idea is where RocketEval starts.

resources.t: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
resources.n: MT-Bench, its 3,355 expert votes (the human judgments RocketEval's agreement numbers use) and the original catalogue of judge biases.

resources.t: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
resources.n: how the Arena Elo ratings that serve as ground truth here are fitted (Bradley-Terry), with bootstrap confidence intervals.
the neighbouring result: a panel of small judges from different families beats one large judge at a fraction of the cost.

resources.t: CheckEval: Robust Evaluation Framework using Large Language Model via Checklist
resources.n: an earlier checklist-of-Boolean-questions evaluator, with fixed, human-curated checklists rather than per-query ones.

resources.t: Prometheus 2: An Open Source Language Model Specialized in Evaluating Other Language Models
resources.n: the fine-tuned 7B judge that RocketEval beats with untuned small models; the other way to make a small judge.
queries, GPT-4o checklists, responses and GPT-4o grades for four benchmarks, and a few example gradings by small judges: the files this page re-analyses.

resources.t: Evaluate an LLM with RocketEval in Colab
resources.n: the authors' notebook: run checklist grading with a small judge end to end on a free GPU.

resources.t: Ollama v0.12.11 release notes: log probabilities
resources.n: 12 November 2025: Ollama's native and OpenAI-compatible APIs return token log probabilities, which is what reading P(Yes) and P(No) on a local model needs.

kb.n: the bias catalogue (position, verbosity, self-preference) that explains why removing the channel works, and where RocketEval sits among judge designs.
the same shape one level up: a written list of principles stands in for human judgment, at training time instead of evaluation time.
a checklist here is a procedural anchor there: writing the procedure down is what transfers, and its misapplication failure mode is the one to expect from a spec the executor half understands.
"expensive artifact, cheap execution" in the harness layer: an expensive run writes a runbook that a cheaper model follows.
a trained model synthesises a harness that a cheaper executor runs: the same economics again.
the serving engine the paper runs its small judges on; prefix caching is what makes grading every checklist item separately cheap.

topics.n: LLM-as-judge and production evaluation engineering: why a per-commit gate should act on aggregates, not on single verdicts.
the models used here as judges and as test models.
speculative decoding: the same economics inverted, a cheap model proposes and an expensive process verifies.
distillation: the weights-level version of paying the big model once and running the small one forever.
MT-Bench, WildBench, AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard, the four benchmarks used here.
